strengths: The paper addresses an important bottleneck in active view selection for neural 3D reconstruction: the high cost of repeatedly training or querying neural rendering models during next-best-view selection.
The proposed idea of predicting viewpoint uncertainty maps directly from an input image is intuitive, computationally appealing, and potentially useful beyond the exact setting studied.

The manuscript is generally clear and includes a concrete pipeline, dataset construction procedure, ablations over uncertainty metrics and selection heuristics, and comparisons against several NeRF-based active view selection baselines.

The reported efficiency gains are substantial: the proposed method avoids iterative neural-rendering retraining at inference time and achieves much lower runtime and resource use than the compared baselines.

The evaluation includes both in-domain and held-out-category settings, plus a transfer experiment where viewpoints selected using uncertainty maps generated from Splatter-Image are used to train NeRF and 3DGS models.
weaknesses: The empirical setting is narrow: all experiments appear to be on synthetic, centered ShapeNet objects with known spherical camera geometry and fixed radius. This substantially limits the strength of the claims about general active view selection and real-world applicability.

The paper lacks very important simple baselines such as random view selection, uniform/farthest-point spherical coverage, oracle coverage heuristics, or category-level learned next-view policies. Without these, it is hard to know whether PUN is learning meaningful uncertainty or mostly approximating a good coverage prior on a simple sphere.

Several claims are overstated. The method is said to match or be comparable to the upper bound, but the reported NeRF ID results show a large gap, e.g. 33.19 vs 36.47 PSNR and 6.96 vs 4.11 MSE. The upper bound itself is also unusual because training and evaluation views are identical, so it is not a standard novel-view upper bound.

The OOD evaluation is too small to convincingly establish generalization: only two held-out categories with 10 instances each are used, and all data still come from the same synthetic ShapeNet/Blender pipeline.

The method still relies on a fixed 48-anchor uncertainty representation and interpolation, so the claim of generalization to arbitrary viewpoints is only partially supported. It samples arbitrary candidates, but their scores are induced from a coarse fixed anchor map.

The supervision signal is a proxy derived from single-view synthesis errors of Splatter-Image, not from actual downstream active reconstruction utility. This may bake in biases of the synthesis backbone, and the paper does not sufficiently analyze when the proxy disagrees with true multi-view reconstruction benefit.

The compute comparison is somewhat unfair or at least incomplete: baselines incur iterative NeRF training by design, while PUN amortizes a large offline dataset/model training cost. The paper should report offline NUM generation/training cost and compare against other amortized or non-iterative selection strategies.

The evaluation protocol uses only 20 selected views and 40 test views on a fixed sphere; no path constraints, collision constraints, pose noise, calibration uncertainty, or real acquisition costs are considered, limiting relevance to robotic active perception.

Some implementation details affecting reproducibility and fairness are under-specified, including baseline adaptation details, candidate sampling variance, statistical significance, exact category splits, and whether validation/test choices influenced heuristic thresholds such as the 0.1 uncertainty cutoff.

strengths: The paper targets an important bottleneck in active view selection for neural 3D reconstruction: repeated retraining/evaluation of NeRF-style uncertainty models is computationally expensive.
The proposed idea of predicting a global uncertainty map directly from an observed image is simple, potentially useful, and yields large inference-time speedups in the reported setting.

The manuscript includes several evaluation dimensions beyond PSNR, including SSIM, LPIPS, mesh/coverage metrics, compute usage, OOD categories, 3DGS transfer, and some ablations over uncertainty metrics and selection policies.
The method is easy to understand at a high level and the authors commit to releasing code, models, and datasets.
weaknesses: The experimental setting is too narrow to support the paper's broad claims. Everything is synthetic ShapeNet, object-centered, with known object center, fixed-radius spherical cameras, and limited category diversity. This is far from the active reconstruction settings emphasized in the motivation.

The main empirical claim that PUN is comparable to the upper bound is overstated. In Table 1, PUN is substantially below the upper bound on key image metrics, e.g. ID PSNR 33.19 vs 36.47 and OOD PSNR 34.74 vs 36.91. The ID improvement over NVF is also tiny and likely within variance for several metrics.

The evaluation omits essential baselines such as random view selection, uniform/farthest-point coverage, learned NBV methods, and recent 3DGS-based active methods that are discussed in related work. Without these, it is unclear whether the method beats strong simple geometric priors under this constrained spherical setup.

The comparison is potentially unfair or incomplete because PUN uses a large offline-generated NUM dataset and trained UPNet, while the compute table reports only inference-time view selection. Dataset generation and model training costs are not included, yet the paper makes strong efficiency claims.

The approach appears to learn dataset/category/viewpoint priors rather than calibrated epistemic uncertainty. The paper does not measure correlation/calibration between predicted UMaps and actual reconstruction errors, nor does it test robustness under distribution shifts beyond two ShapeNet categories.

The construction of UMaps is conceptually muddled: PSNR is used as an uncertainty measure although higher PSNR normally means lower error; normalization, thresholding at 0.1, and aggregation by products are not sufficiently justified or clearly specified.

The upper-bound protocol is questionable: it trains on the same 40 views used for evaluation, making it an idealized reconstruction/evaluation overlap rather than a meaningful upper bound for novel view synthesis.

Generalization evidence is weak. The OOD setting contains only two categories with 10 instances each, and still within ShapeNet and the same camera/object assumptions. This does not justify claims about novel object categories or arbitrary viewpoints.

The 3DGS result is striking but under-analyzed: no upper bound, random/coverage baseline, or explanation is provided, and the baselines are NeRF-oriented view selectors being judged through 3DGS reconstruction.

Ablations are limited and sometimes do not strongly support the conclusions. For example, several selection-policy variants are close, and the paper does not ablate UPNet architecture, training data size realistically, interpolation choices, candidate sampling density, or initial view sensitivity.

Reproducibility details are incomplete: hyperparameters, training schedules, exact splits, random seeds, baseline implementation details, and full offline data generation costs are not sufficiently specified in the main text.

There are notable clarity and polish issues, including inconsistent citations for NeRF/3DGS references, typos, unclear notation in the aggregation equation, and occasional overclaiming relative to the reported numbers.

strengths: Clear and useful problem framing: predicting neural uncertainty maps with a lightweight feedforward model is a compelling way to avoid repeated NeRF/3DGS retraining during active view selection.

The efficiency gains are substantial and well aligned with the motivation: the reported viewpoint-selection time drops from roughly 175-198 minutes for baselines to 0.5 minutes, with large reductions in CPU/GPU memory and utilization.

The paper provides a coherent dataset construction pipeline, a concrete selection algorithm, ablations over uncertainty metrics and aggregation policies, and evaluations with both NeRF and 3DGS backends.

Results are encouraging, especially in the OOD ShapeNet setting and in the 3DGS evaluation, where the selected views transfer well despite UPNet being trained using Splatter-Image-derived uncertainty maps.
The method is interpretable: uncertainty maps over candidate viewpoints make the policy easier to inspect than black-box next-view predictors.
weaknesses: The main claim that PUN matches the upper bound is overstated. In Table 1, the upper bound is still clearly better on PSNR, LPIPS, MSE, and visibility; in the ID setting PUN improves only marginally over NVF on several metrics, e.g. 33.19 vs. 33.08 PSNR and 6.96 vs. 6.98 MSE.

The evaluation is restricted to synthetic, object-centered ShapeNet scenes with known radius and spherical camera distributions. This limits evidence for applicability to robotics, real-world scanning, cluttered scenes, or arbitrary environments.
OOD generalization is tested on only two unseen categories with 10 instances each, which is too narrow to fully support broad generalization claims.

The comparison may favor PUN in computational cost because PUN amortizes training through a supervised offline NUM dataset, while baselines perform online uncertainty estimation. The paper should more clearly account for NUM generation/training cost and discuss deployment assumptions.

Some methodological details raise questions: PUN predicts uncertainty on only 48 anchors but claims support for arbitrary viewpoints via interpolation; candidate views are still sampled on a fixed object-centered sphere; and the 0.1 redundancy threshold appears heuristic.
The dataset split description appears inconsistent: the text says 80/10/10 train/validation/test per category, while the supplement figure caption describes 90 training instances for 11 categories.

Reproducibility is incomplete at submission time: code, models, and datasets are promised but not yet available, and several implementation details for baselines and fairness of their adaptation are not fully specified.

strengths: The paper addresses an important bottleneck in active view selection for neural 3D reconstruction: avoiding repeated expensive NeRF/3DGS retraining during view planning.

The core idea of predicting a view-conditioned uncertainty map with a feed-forward network is intuitive, potentially useful, and much more computationally efficient at inference than model-based uncertainty baselines.
The evaluation covers several axes: seen-category novel instances, held-out categories, altered lighting/camera distance, different reconstruction backbones, and small tests on NeRFAssets/MIP360.
The paper includes useful ablations on uncertainty metrics, aggregation policies, training-data composition, anchor density, and redundancy thresholds.
The reported runtime/resource gains are substantial and, if reproducible, would make the method practically attractive.
weaknesses: The main performance gains over the strongest baseline are modest in the primary NUM-inst setting, and the reported standard deviations suggest some differences may not be statistically meaningful; mesh-quality gains are also weak or absent.

The claimed comparison to the upper bound is overstated: PUN remains notably below the upper bound on image metrics in the main tables, and the upper-bound protocol trains/tests on the same views, making it an unusual and not very informative reference point.

The method relies on substantial offline supervision from ShapeNet, Splatter-Image, rendered ground truth, and generated uncertainty maps, but the evaluation does not fully account for this offline cost or compare against similarly amortized learned view-selection methods.
Reproducibility is incomplete: the manuscript says code, models, and datasets are available, but the URL is blank in both the abstract and reproducibility statement.

The setup is still quite constrained: object-centered spherical camera motion, fixed radius in most experiments, random candidate sampling, and 48-anchor interpolation. This weakens claims about arbitrary viewpoints and unconstrained realistic active reconstruction.

The real-scene evidence is limited to four selected MIP360 scenes with target-centered views and no geometry metrics, so generalization to realistic robotic or scene-level exploration remains under-supported.

Several technical details are underspecified or potentially fragile, including the exact normalization/sign convention for PSNR-based uncertainty, interpolation behavior when few anchors fall within 30 degrees, baseline hyperparameter parity, and statistical testing.

The novelty is incremental relative to learned next-best-view and uncertainty-prediction pipelines: the paper’s main distinction is the neural uncertainty map representation and amortized selection, but the conceptual advance may not be broad enough without stronger validation.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and practical problem: reducing the high cost of active view selection for neural 3D reconstruction.

The basic idea of amortizing next-view selection through a feedforward network that predicts an uncertainty landscape is plausible and potentially useful, especially compared with methods that retrain a NeRF-like model after each selected view.
The manuscript includes several ablations and evaluates multiple reconstruction backbones, uncertainty metrics, and environmental variants, which is a good direction.
Reported runtime and resource reductions are large, suggesting that the approach could be practically attractive if the evaluation were made more convincing.
weaknesses: The central empirical claims are overstated. The paper repeatedly says PUN is comparable to or matches the all-view upper bound, but the reported numbers show clear gaps, e.g. 33.19 vs 36.47 PSNR on NUM-inst and 34.74 vs 36.91 on NUM-cat. This is not a minor difference, and the upper-bound setup itself is unusual because it trains and tests on the same 40 views.

The evaluation is not sufficiently convincing for a top-tier venue. Most evidence is on synthetic ShapeNet-derived data with controlled spherical camera assumptions. The claimed real-scene generalization is based on only four NeRFAssets and four MIP360 scenes, and is compared only to NVF in the main realistic-scene table.

There are fairness concerns in the efficiency comparison. PUN relies on a supervised offline NUM dataset generated with Blender and Splatter-Image, plus UPNet training, but the runtime comparison emphasizes only test-time selection while baselines perform iterative model training. The offline cost and data assumptions are not properly accounted for.

The method is less general than claimed. Although the paper says it generalizes to arbitrary viewpoints, UPNet predicts only a 48-anchor uncertainty vector and arbitrary candidates are handled by interpolation. The setup also assumes a single centered object, known object-centric spherical camera geometry, and fixed-radius candidate views.

The uncertainty formulation is under-specified and potentially confused. PSNR is described as an uncertainty measure, but higher PSNR normally means lower reconstruction error; the paper does not clearly explain the transformation/sign convention used before selecting the maximum uncertainty. This ambiguity affects the technical soundness of the core selection rule.

Several conclusions are not supported by the tables. The paper claims PUN outperforms all baselines across all eight metrics, but full results show cases where other methods match or exceed it on mesh completion or visual coverage, and the gains over NVF on NUM-inst image metrics are very small relative to reported variance.

The novelty is incremental. Learning a direct predictor for view utility/uncertainty is a reasonable engineering contribution, but the method largely combines a pretrained ViT regressor, synthetic supervision from reconstruction error, interpolation, and heuristic aggregation. The paper does not establish a substantially new principle for AVS.

Reproducibility is weak as written: the code/model/dataset availability statement is blank, important implementation choices are missing or ambiguous, and some experimental details such as candidate sampling consistency, baseline tuning, and offline NUM generation cost are not sufficiently documented.

The paper contains presentation issues and imprecise claims, including exaggerated wording, inconsistent capitalization/naming, typos in ablation labels, and some vague causal explanations for why UPNet generalizes. These do not alone determine the score, but they compound the more serious evaluation and soundness concerns.

strengths: Clear and practically relevant contribution: predicting neural uncertainty maps with a feedforward model is an appealing way to avoid iterative NeRF/3DGS retraining during active view selection.
The method is simple, interpretable, and computationally compelling; the reported viewpoint-selection runtime/resource reductions over NeRF-based uncertainty baselines are substantial.

The experimental suite is broader than many AVS papers, covering novel ShapeNet instances/categories, altered lighting and camera distance, multiple reconstruction backbones, and small real/realistic scene evaluations.
Ablations cover several important design choices, including uncertainty metric, aggregation/removal policy, anchor count, thresholding, and training-data diversity versus viewpoint density.
The proposed NUM dataset/resource could be useful to the community if actually released with code and pretrained models.
weaknesses: The empirical claims are somewhat stronger than the evidence. On NUM-inst, the gain over NVF is very small for PSNR/MSE and within large variance for some metrics, while the paper repeatedly claims matching the upper bound despite sizable PSNR/LPIPS gaps in Tables 1/S1.
The upper-bound protocol is unusual and partly misleading: it trains on the same 40 views used for evaluation, making it less a realistic upper bound than a near-oracle reconstruction setting.

Generalization evidence is promising but limited. NeRFAssets and MIP360 use only four scenes each, and comparisons there are only against NVF, not the full baseline set or recent 3DGS active reconstruction methods such as ActiveGS/ActiveGAMER.
Reproducibility is currently weak: the abstract and reproducibility statement say code/models/datasets are available, but the manuscript leaves the URL blank.

The method depends on a large offline UMap-generation pipeline using Splatter-Image pretrained on ShapeNet; the runtime comparison does not account for this amortized training/data-generation cost, which matters for new domains.

The novelty is incremental in spirit: learning a direct proxy for next-view uncertainty is useful, but the core selection rule is heuristic and the paper does not deeply compare against learned NBV policies or simpler learned regressors/classifiers that might provide similar benefits.

Some technical details are underspecified or potentially confusing, including how PSNR is converted into an uncertainty signal, normalization across metrics/maps, and how candidate sampling randomness affects reported results.
